interactions.summary: A student says Dante reduces fear by turning the unknown afterlife into something knowable, acting as a tour guide through hell and heaven so terror loses some of its grip.

Jiang rejects a merely instructional model, saying that universities and preaching already tried to remove fear without success; he presses toward the idea that Dante must live the truth and that the Divine Comedy itself is the proof.
A student offers free will and destiny as evidence that God loves human beings, but Jiang immediately treats this as abstract logic rather than the convincing force he is asking about.
Jiang sharpens the distinction again: if Dante simply lectured that God is love, no one would care, so the class has to explain why the poem can persuade where argument fails.
A student says the audience must go on the journey with Dante, embodying the experience rather than just hearing a proposition.
Jiang turns from the poem to a more basic question: what art is, and why art differs from other kinds of discourse.

speaker_notes.note: The student's sentence is clipped, but the stable point is an appeal to free will or destiny as rational proof that God loves human beings.

claims.claim: A student says Dante reduces fear by making the unknown afterlife knowable through the guided journey of the poem.
Jiang says direct teaching against fear would fail because scholastic and mendicant attempts already tried that route without changing people.
Jiang pushes the class toward the claim that Dante must live the truth of God's love and that the Divine Comedy itself is the medium that proves it.
A student's appeal to free will as evidence of divine love is treated by Jiang as insufficient because it remains only logical or discursive.
A student says the Divine Comedy persuades because readers are made to go on the same journey Dante undergoes rather than merely hear an argument.
Jiang frames the next step of the lecture as defining art itself in order to explain why poetry can do what theology lectures cannot.

signature_moments.moment: The student casts Dante as a guide who turns the terrifying unknown into something seen and navigable.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he's turning the unknown into a known
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the poem a practical anti-fear mechanism instead of treating it as abstract doctrine.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang insists that the truth that God is love cannot simply be lectured; it has to be lived and artistically enacted until people undergo it.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the hinge between doctrinal statement and poetic transformation.

signature_moments.moment: The student's answer locates the poem's persuasive power in the fact that the audience is taken on the journey with Dante.
signature_moments.source_phrase: let the readers or the audience go on the journey
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It names participation as the mechanism by which art reshapes fear and belief.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The student's formula for how Dante reduces fear: by rendering the feared afterlife imaginable and narratable.
Jiang's shorthand for the difference between declarative teaching and embodied proof.
The participatory structure by which the poem persuades readers rather than merely informing them.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-17 Jiang shifts from historical fear and divine love into an aesthetic mechanism: the Divine Comedy works not as a lecture but as lived, artistic proof that must be undergone by readers.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's free-will answer is syntactically broken, so the extraction keeps only the stable contrast between abstract logic and the embodied proof Jiang wants.
